strengths: Timely and relevant contribution: the paper targets a genuine gap — unified evaluation for text-to-audio-video generation — and Table 1 convincingly shows that prior benchmarks (VBench, JavisBench, VABench, etc.) lack instruction-following and realism dimensions.

Well-structured dual-level evaluation design: combining objective signal metrics (DOVER++, CLAP, VideoCLIP-XL, ImageBind, Synchformer/DeSync) with a reasoning-first MLLM-as-a-Judge protocol using granular QA checklists and violation checks (e.g., Material-Timbre Consistency) improves interpretability over prior work.

Broad empirical coverage: evaluation of 11 systems including recent proprietary models (Veo-3.1, Sora-2, Kling-2.6) and composed pipelines, with fine-grained per-sub-dimension breakdowns in Tables 2-4 that yield useful diagnostic findings such as the 'Audio Realism Bottleneck'.

Strong reproducibility effort in the appendix: full judge and rewriting prompts are provided (Appendix G), decoding is deterministic (temperature=0, do_sample=False), dataset construction details (dedup threshold, square-root sampling, video filtering criteria) are documented, and limitations are honestly discussed (Appendix A).
weaknesses: No human validation of the core MLLM-as-a-Judge protocol. The paper's central claims about model realism and instruction following rest entirely on Gemini-2.5-Pro judgments, yet there is no human agreement study, no correlation with human ratings, and no ablation across alternative judge models. This is a decisive evidential gap for a benchmark whose headline results are subjective scores.

Potential judge bias and circularity: the same model (Gemini-2.5-Pro) is used to rewrite prompts, generate the QA checklists, and serve as the judge. Checklists are constructed so the expected answer is always 'Yes', which may systematically penalize weaker models and is never analyzed. The judge's ability to actually perceive audio (e.g., to score Material-Timbre Consistency or Acoustic Artifacts) is not established.

Confounded cross-model comparisons: models are evaluated at different resolutions (JavisDiT at 480p, Kling-2.6 at 1080p, others at 720p) with different frame rates, and prompts for Ovi-1.1 and composed pipelines are paraphrased by Gemini while others are not. These setup differences can materially affect both objective and subjective scores, undermining the ranking conclusions.

The collected 'realism ceiling' reference set of 100 real YouTube videos (Appendix F.2) is never actually used in the reported results; grounding the judge scores against real videos would have substantially strengthened validity. Similarly, Section C 'More Detailed Results' is empty, suggesting incompleteness.

Missing statistical rigor: it is unclear whether each prompt is generated once or multiple times per model; closed-source systems are stochastic, yet no variance, confidence intervals, or significance analysis is reported. Metric normalization is also unclear (VT scores around 7-13 for DOVER++, PQ/CU scales) and the DS offset_sec of -2.0 is arbitrary and unmotivated.

The benchmark size (500 prompts, only 100 from grounded video inversion) is modest, and the 'Audio Realism Bottleneck' finding largely re-confirms what the community already suspects; the added scientific insight beyond the taxonomy and checklist design is limited.

Several presentation issues reduce polish: inconsistent metric definitions across Sections 3.3.1, 3.3.2, and Appendix D.2 (e.g., TCS, OIS, AAS described differently), the unexplained 'a b' superscripts in the abstract, and figures with very small fonts (Figures 1, 5, 6).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and genuinely under-served evaluation gap: unified assessment of text-to-audio-video generation spanning video quality, audio quality, cross-modal alignment, instruction following, and realism.

The prompt construction pipeline is documented in reasonable detail (semantic deduplication, square-root sampling, LLM rewriting with human audit, video-inversion stream with anti-overfitting date filtering), and the QA checklist extraction prompts are fully disclosed in the appendix, which aids reproducibility of the taxonomy.

The taxonomy of instruction-following dimensions (7 primary / 17 sub-dimensions) and the realism criteria (MSS, OIS, TCS, AAS, MTC) are concretely defined with scoring rubrics (Tables 5-7), giving the framework interpretability.
The evaluation covers 11 representative systems including leading proprietary models, and the fine-grained sub-dimension breakdowns (Table 4) allow diagnostic analysis.
The limitations section is candid about MLLM-judge biases, computational overhead, and prompt-scale constraints.
weaknesses: The central evaluation mechanism is unvalidated. All subjective results (Tables 3-4, Figures 5-6) derive solely from Gemini-2.5-Pro acting as judge, yet no human study is reported to verify that judge scores correlate with human judgment. Headline claims (e.g., models 'fall substantially short of human-level realism', the 'Audio Realism Bottleneck') therefore rest entirely on an uncorroborated automated protocol.

Potential circularity and bias: Gemini-2.5-Pro is used both to generate/rewrite the benchmark prompts and to judge model outputs against checklists derived from those same prompts. A judge scoring content against criteria it authored is a known source of systematic bias, and no mitigation or sensitivity analysis (e.g., alternative judges) is provided.

Unfair experimental conditions across systems: resolutions differ (480p for Javis, 720p default, 1080p for Kling-2.6), and only Ovi-1.1 and composed pipelines receive Gemini-2.5-Pro prompt paraphrasing, which plausibly advantages or disadvantages specific systems in instruction-following scores. These confounds are acknowledged but not controlled or ablated.

Limited novelty over existing T2AV benchmarks. Table 1 itself lists JavisBench, Verse-Bench, Harmony-Bench, UniAVGen, and VABench already covering VQ/AQ/CMA dimensions; the incremental contribution (longer prompts, more sub-dimensions, additional metrics) is assembled from off-the-shelf metrics (DOVER++, LAION-Aesthetic, CLAP, VideoCLIP-XL, ImageBind, Synchformer) with no evidence these are reliable for generated content in this setting.

Small and partly synthetic prompt set: only 500 prompts, of which 400 are LLM-rewritten community prompts and 100 are video inversions; no ablation of how prompt-rewrite distribution shift affects measured model failures.

No statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, variance across judge runs, inter-rater (multi-judge) agreement, or significance testing for the rankings reported in Tables 2-3, despite deterministic-decoding claims that could support at least run-to-run stability checks.

Incomplete manuscript: Section C 'More Detailed Results' is empty, Section D.1 'Instruction Following' is empty, Section 3.1 contains a grammatical fragment ('video inversion at, as shown'), Section 2 references 'Figure 4(e)' though Figure 4 has no (e) panel, and the introduction contains 'our contributions are threshold as follows'. These editorial lapses undermine confidence in overall care.

The claimed distinction that prompts have higher average token counts (154 vs. 50-68 for baselines) is presented as a benefit, but no evidence is offered that longer prompts measure anything beyond models' prompt-length sensitivity, and the tokenization choice (Qwen3) is not justified relative to how each proprietary model actually tokenizes prompts.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated contribution: unified evaluation of text-to-audio-video generation addresses a genuine gap, and the comparison of dimensions in Table 1 clearly positions T2AV-Compass against unimodal and concurrent joint A/V benchmarks (JavisBench, VABench, Verse-Bench, Harmony-Bench).

Comprehensive empirical study: 11 systems spanning closed-source end-to-end models, open-source models, and composed pipelines (T2V+TV2A, T2A+TA2V), with both objective signal metrics and MLLM-based subjective tracks; the fine-grained sub-dimension breakdowns (Tables 4-7) provide real diagnostic value.

Thoughtful data curation design: taxonomy-driven clustering with square-root sampling, deduplication, anti-overfitting filtering of post-October-2024 video references, and a documented difficulty analysis (subject multiplicity, on/off-screen audio, event chains) that supports the claim of a more challenging prompt distribution.

Strong transparency on the evaluation protocol: the complete judge prompts (IF checklists per dimension, MSS/OIS/TCS/AAS/MTC rubrics), deterministic decoding settings, and frame-sampling rates are disclosed, aiding reproducibility of the subjective protocol. Limitations (MLLM bias, cost, prompt coverage) are honestly discussed.

Concrete and actionable findings, e.g., the 'Audio Realism Bottleneck' and the observation that composed pipelines can exceed end-to-end models on Video Realism, which are useful signals for the field.
weaknesses: Central claims rest on an unvalidated single-model judge: all subjective scores (Table 3, the Audio Realism Bottleneck headline finding) come from Gemini-2.5-Pro alone, with no human study, no inter-rater or judge-human correlation, and no ablation across alternative judges. For a benchmark whose main methodological novelty is the MLLM-as-a-Judge protocol, this is a significant evidential gap.

Circularity in the construction/evaluation loop: prompts are rewritten by Gemini-2.5-Pro, QA checklists are extracted by the same model, and judging is again performed by the same model. This risks a systematic bias where the judge grades prompts in a style it itself authored, and it is not analyzed or mitigated in the paper.

Presentation and completeness problems undermine polish and reproducibility: Appendix C 'More Detailed Results' is empty, Section D.1 'Instruction Following' is empty, D.2 defines TCS/OIS differently than the main text (TCS 'Temporal Continuity' vs 'Temporal Coherence Score'; OIS 'Object Identity Stability' vs 'Object Integrity Score'), and there is no explicit statement that code, prompts, or the benchmark will be released.

Potential fairness/confound issues in the comparison are not analyzed: models are evaluated at different resolutions (480p for Javis, 1080p for Kling-2.6, 720p default) which directly affects DOVER++/aesthetic scores, and prompts for Ovi-1.1 and composed pipelines are paraphrased by Gemini, which may advantage or disadvantage specific systems; no sensitivity analysis is provided.

Discriminative power of objective metrics is weak: T-A/T-V/A-V similarity values cluster in a narrow band (~0.13-0.29) across very different systems, and no correlation between objective metrics and human preference or the subjective tracks is reported, leaving unclear whether the objective pillar measures anything the field cares about.

The 'first comprehensive benchmark' framing is overstated given the multiple concurrent T2AV benchmarks discussed; single generation run per prompt is not discussed (variance of generative outputs is ignored), and the judge's known biases (style/frequency preferences, acknowledged in Limitations) are not quantified.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: unified, diagnostic evaluation of text-to-audio-video generation, with coverage of instruction following and realism that prior T2AV benchmarks (JavisBench, VABench, Verse-Bench) lack

Careful dataset construction pipeline (multi-source collection, embedding deduplication, square-root sampling for long-tail coverage, video-inversion stream with human verification) is well documented, and prompt complexity (154 avg tokens, 4.03 subjects, 3.61 events) demonstrably exceeds prior benchmarks

Dual-level evaluation framework is comprehensive: objective signal metrics (DOVER++, CLAP, ImageBind, Synchformer, LatentSync) plus a checklist-based MLLM-as-judge protocol with a 7-dimension/17-sub-dimension taxonomy

Unusually thorough validation of the judge: human-MLLM agreement on 50 prompts/250 samples, forced-choice pairwise comparisons fit with Bradley-Terry/Elo, judge-stability analysis (CV, Spearman across Gemini variants), and an upper-bound calibration using 100 real-world videos that shows the judge is not 'over-praising'

Generates useful empirical insights: monotonic failure-rate growth with subject/event complexity (63-80% failure on long-narrative prompts), audio-realism bottleneck, and sound-effects being the hardest audio sub-dimension

Honest limitations section explicitly acknowledges MLLM judge bias, closed-source Gemini dependence, version drift, and prompt-scale limits, and positions the judge as a scalable proxy rather than an oracle
weaknesses: Potential circularity/self-preference bias: Gemini-2.5-Pro is used both to rewrite prompts and extract checklists (data construction) and as the primary judge (evaluation), and Gemini-2.5-Pro also achieves the best human agreement; cross-family judge disagreement is substantial (L1 1.32-1.48), so the headline leaderboard could be tilted toward Gemini-adjacent pipelines; the paper does not test a non-Gemini judge on the full suite
Human validation is thin relative to the claims: agreement and pairwise-preference studies cover only 50 prompts and 5 models, with 5 annotators; all other conclusions rest on the automated judge

Evaluation protocol fairness concerns: prompts are Gemini-paraphrased only for Ovi-based and composed-pipeline systems, and native resolution varies (480p for Javis vs 1080p for Kling-2.6), which may confound comparisons across systems

Reporting and metric inconsistencies: Table 4/6 headers use ↑ arrows for L1 distance while the text says lower is better; Table 2 mixes incomparable raw scales (VT~13, VA~5, AA~6, DS~0.7s) with no stated normalization, making cross-column reading misleading; the IF-Audio penalty term (P = 1 - S_nonspeech) is ad hoc and its sensitivity is not analyzed

Benchmark scale is modest (500 prompts) and prompt generation is heavily templated via a single LLM rewriting prompt, which risks stylistic/coverage biases toward Gemini-authored descriptive conventions
Contemporaneous overlap with VABench and Verse-Bench reduces originality of the core idea; the delta is mainly the taxonomy density, checklist protocol, and diagnostic analyses

Release/reproducibility details are incompletely stated in the text (the code/HuggingFace link is a placeholder in the manuscript), so reproducibility cannot be fully verified from the paper alone, and judge dependence on a closed-source, version-drifting API limits long-term reproducibility

strengths: Timely and practically relevant: unified T2AV evaluation addressing a real fragmentation problem, with coverage of video quality, audio quality, cross-modal alignment, instruction following, and realism dimensions that existing benchmarks (Table 1) largely do not combine.

Large-scale empirical study: 15 systems spanning closed-source end-to-end models, open-source models, and cascaded pipelines, with fine-grained sub-dimension breakdowns (Tables 5-6) that yield genuinely useful diagnostics, e.g., the long-narrative failure escalation (63-80%) and cascaded pipelines being strong-but-disjoint.

The authors validate the judge rather than merely asserting it: human-MLLM agreement (Tables 4, 6), Bradley-Terry/Elo ranking validation (Tables 8-9), judge robustness across Gemini variants (Spearman rho = 0.9248), metric orthogonality analysis (Fig. 9), preprocessing sensitivity tests, and an upper-bound calibration on 100 real videos (D.6).

Honest and detailed limitations section (Appendix A), including closed-source judge dependence, vendor drift, and prompt-scale constraints; evaluation prompts and rubrics are reproduced in the appendix.
weaknesses: Circularity between benchmark construction and evaluation: Gemini-2.5-Pro is used to rewrite prompts, generate the QA checklists, judge instruction following, and score realism. A judge judging its own rewritten prompts and its own generated checklists risks systematic leniency/bias that the human agreement study (50 prompts) cannot rule out.

The headline finding, the 'Audio Realism Bottleneck,' rests on the weakest-validated judge dimension: the authors' own analysis (Table 6) shows audio realism has by far the worst human-MLLM agreement (+36.3% L1 gap for Gemini-2.5-Pro, +61% for Qwen3-Omni), and the upper-bound analysis (D.6) itself admits the judge is 'overly critical' of even authentic recordings (Sound Effects ceiling 83.50 on real videos). Attributing a model deficiency via an instrument that demonstrably mis-measures that dimension is not sound.

Limited incremental originality: the field already contains several concurrent audio-video benchmarks (JavisBench, VABench, Verse-Bench, Harmony-Bench per Table 1). The delta over VABench in particular (which also combines expert metrics and MLLM-based evaluation across T2AV settings) is mostly longer prompts and more checklist dimensions, yet the paper claims to be 'the first comprehensive benchmark.'

Human validation is thin: only 50 prompts, 5 annotators, 250 samples for the primary claim of judge reliability; the reported inter-human L1 (~0.91-1.04 on a 1-5 scale) is itself substantial, making 'near-human' framing of Gemini-2.5-Pro (L1 1.087) questionable, and no confidence intervals are given for the difficulty/failure-rate analyses (only 3 models analyzed in Fig. 8).

Fair-comparison concerns in Table 2: models run at heterogeneous resolutions (JavisDiT at 480p, Kling-2.6 at 1080p) despite resolution-sensitive metrics (DOVER VT); a subset of models is evaluated with Gemini-paraphrased prompts while others use originals; and 'some videos are not generated successfully' due to security review is unquantified, so per-model prompt coverage may differ. The reported VT range (6.85-13.43) is also unexplained and looks inconsistent with standard DOVER output.

Contamination is not credibly controlled: prompts are aggregated from Kling AI community and LMArena and then rewritten, and model APIs may have seen similar distributions; the anti-leakage measure (post-Oct-2024 YouTube content) applies only to the inversion stream, not the 400 community prompts.

Reproducibility is weakened in the main text: the availability sentence reads 'Code and data are available at [blank] and HuggingFace' with a missing link; the judge is a closed-source commercial model with known version drift, which the authors acknowledge but which limits independent verification even with released data.

Presentation issues: Figures 4 and 11 are near-duplicates, and the caption of Figure 3(a) refers to 'T2AVBench' rather than T2AV-Compass, suggesting rushed preparation; several analyses (e.g., difficulty trends) are only on a 3-model subset without justification.

strengths: Timely and clearly motivated problem: T2AV evaluation is genuinely fragmented (unimodal metrics, narrow benchmarks), and the paper provides a unified testbed covering video quality, audio quality, cross-modal alignment, instruction following, and realism.

Well-constructed prompt suite: the three-stage pipeline (multi-source collection, LLM rewriting with human refinement, YouTube video-inversion with human-in-the-loop verification) is sensible, and prompts are substantially longer/more complex (154 avg tokens, more subjects/events) than competing benchmarks (Table 1).

Dual-level evaluation design is thoughtful: objective expert metrics (DOVER++, NISQA, CLAP, ImageBind, Synchformer, LatentSync) plus checklist-based MLLM-as-judge with reasoning-first protocol; judge prompts, dimension taxonomies (7 primary/17 sub-dimensions), and scoring formulas are all released, aiding reproducibility.

Unusually thorough validation for a benchmark paper: human–MLLM agreement analysis with L1 distances and inter-human baselines (Table 6), Bradley–Terry pairwise ranking that matches human ordering (D.5), judge robustness via repeated runs (CV ≤ 1.02%, Spearman ρ = 0.9248), metric-redundancy analysis via de-meaned correlations (Fig. 9), preprocessing/sampling-rate sensitivity checks, and an upper-bound calibration on real-world videos (Fig. 10).

Empirically rich and diagnostic results: evaluation of 15 systems including leading proprietary models yields useful findings (Audio Realism Bottleneck, Dynamics bottleneck, monotonic failure escalation with subject/event complexity, cascaded pipelines strong but misaligned), and the paper is appropriately cautious, framing causal attributions as diagnostic evidence.
Honest limitations section (judge computational cost, MLLM biases, closed-source judge dependency, prompt-scale limits) and a reasonable impact statement.
weaknesses: Potential circularity between prompt construction and judging: Gemini-2.5-Pro both rewrites/generates most prompts and serves as the judge of instruction following on checklists derived from those same prompts; while human refinement and the video-inversion stream mitigate this, the paper does not directly measure or discuss this bias source.

The core human validation is small: the agreement study covers only 50 prompts (250 samples) and 5 models; the notable +36.3% gap for Gemini-2.5-Pro on Audio Realism means one of the headline findings (the Audio Realism Bottleneck) rests partly on a judge dimension where judge–human agreement is weakest, even though this is acknowledged.

Some objective metric reporting is under-specified or of unclear scale: e.g., VT scores range 6.85–13.43 although DOVER technical quality is conventionally in [0,1]; several alignment scores (T-V ~0.24, A-V ~0.13–0.29) have very small dynamic ranges with no demonstration that the between-model differences are meaningful; the 5-point Likert-to-score mapping and 'compact Average' aggregation also deserve more scrutiny.

Comparability/fairness concerns in the model evaluation setup: Kling-2.6 is run at 1080p while JavisDiT at 480p, and prompts for Ovi-1.1-based and composed systems are paraphrased by Gemini before generation, which could confound cross-model comparisons despite the authors' intent.

Overlapping novelty: VABench and JavisBench already offer joint audio-video evaluation with MLLM-based metrics; T2AV-Compass's advantages (longer compositional prompts, IF/RE dimensions, diagnostic checklists) are real but incremental, so the 'first comprehensive benchmark' framing is somewhat overstated.

Minor presentation issues: Table 4/6 use upward arrows on columns where lower is better (L1 distance); some citations have implausible dates (LTX-2, arXiv:2601.03233, 2026); several appendix sections (G) are placeholders; no statistical significance testing on the 500-prompt metric comparisons.
The failure-rate analysis (Fig. 8) covers only three models; extending it to more systems would strengthen the difficulty-complexity conclusions.
